results.rawContent:
Today’s post is primarily for more committed wine consumers who regularly buy wines from some of the more distinctive appellations of France and Italy. No weighty issues to discuss (well, a couple of exceptions to that may come up in the discussion below!). Like my previous exposés on the wines of Kysela Pere et Fils and the Wines of Georgia ,today’s verbiage centers on a recent portfolio tasting offered by one of the pioneering, quality-oriented, importers in America; Kermit Lynch. Future tastings like this (‘tis the season) will also be covered.
The reason I write up these notes is because so many people I know from my decades in retail, restaurant buying and importing are very curious about wines they have heard of, perhaps, but are not able to taste or purchase, often due to poor distribution and unavailability. Today, with the internet and operations like Wine-searcher.com or Vivino.com, it is far easier to find wines like these. We have a number of fine wine importers across the country, many of whom only work in local markets. Kermit Lynch is one whose wines are available more or less, nationally.
But how does one choose? There are 1000’s of new imported wines entering our market every year; Some good, some great, some meh! There are a few importers like Lynch, however, whose selections generally speaking are reliable and worthy of consideration. Not every wine of course is a star, but most are consistently interesting and reflect the care and intelligence of their makers.
Tasting a wide range of wines from the same importer can provide insight into the style preference and what that person(s) quality values are, whether it be concentration, high profile appellations, heightened ‘wine-making, ‘natural-ness’ (?), refinement and finesse, or terroir expression-a sense of place and tradition.
I have known Kermit Lynch practically from when he opened his tiny storefront in Berkeley in 1972, which was the same year I began my journey in the wine trade. I have been a customer, individual and business-wise, and a (friendly critic when necessary of his for decades. I have great respect for his efforts to turn wine lovers on to authentic versions of his favored wine regions, originally just France, and now increasingly from Italy,too.
Kermit has also shown himself to be a deft writer about wine ( Adventures on the Wine Route) and his philosophy which strongly depends on forming a personal connection with those growers and winemakers he works with. He came into the wine business informed by his travels in Europe, and I suppose, some disillusionment about the quality and commercialization of California wines, the ‘low-bar' set by then giants of the industry, and the dearth, 50+ years ago, of small production fine wine producers available in America.
In Europe, I think it safe to say, (certainly I found it to be true from my own peregrinations there in the early 70’s), Lynch began to search for people who were strongly connected to their land and culture, their traditional styles. I know that his meeting people like Lucien and Lulu Peyraud at Domaine Tempier and tasting their benchmark, but slightly rustic wines from the backwoods appellation of Bandol in Provence was an epiphany.
Lynch built upon that relationship to forge long-lasting ties to other emerging producers whose wines reflected anti-industrial, anti-bureaucratic and pro-terroir driven approaches to making characterful wines; expressions of their land, and at least somewhat, their own personalities. Most of his selections lean towards low intervention production methods, but he is no Luddite; “natural wines”, so called, only enter the catalogue if attentively made.
This philosophy continues with Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant (KLWM) as Kermit himself has stepped back from day to day work leaving that to his son, Anthony. The portfolio over the years has grown hugely from what I remember 50+ years ago. ( There is more professionalism and smoother operations, but the basic perspective has not really changed.
That said, what has changed over the years is the business itself. What started out as a small selective wine retail store in Berkeley, where prices were quite reasonable in general, since the wines were directly imported by Kermit, bypassing a distributor (the outdated three-tier system) outgrew its initial business niche. Kermit Lynch had then one of the only ‘grandfathered’ in licenses to both directly import and retail sell his wines in CA. In those days, there was virtually no wine-shipping outside of California. Thus, he could sell a quality Côtes du Rhône for $4 when his competitors had to sell theirs for at least $6 or more.
But when Lynch found that his supply chain, his group of producers were growing, he realized that he could no longer sell everything out of a single store and thus ‘undercut’ others offering better value for quality. So began Lynch’s journey to national recognition and distribution. Therefore, this meant having to work with distributors in other states, and even countries, where people were desirous of having his selections on their shelves and restaurant lists. Which meant, too, your pricing had to change to reflect your inability to undercut (i.e. offer better quality/price rapport) others AND factor in the profit margins required by your new distributor/retail accounts for them to accept your wines.
I don’t know factually what Kermit was thinking as he was confronted by this new reality, but I suspect it annoyed the hell out of him. Losing the opportunity to offer better value, better wines to consumers because of an archaic, protectionist, anti-consumer distribution system imposed constitutionally is a grating proposition at best!
Anyway, here we are today. The KLWM showcases some of the best and widely known regions of France and Italy, as well as some little-known ones that the current buyers (no longer just Kermit) find intrinsically delicious and interesting. I don’t agree with some of their choices, especially those whose prices stretch my credibility for a relatively unproven place. I also find some of these selections below over-priced, which I note. Qualitatively they are excellent (also noted), but seriously, few consumers are in a position to buy and enjoy wines without feeling guilty that cost today $50+ when only just a few years ago they were half that price or less.
Sigh! IT’s the market, I recognize. Burgundy especially is no longer an affordable option for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay lovers, with few exceptions. And KLWM has never been shy about asking a good return for their wine selections. But over the many years I have known Kermit, his company and wines, there was generally a feeling that ‘our’ wines should be accessible for a wide range of customers. That company strength of decades ago is no longer so evident, through often no fault of KLWM. It is getting harder to find everyday priced quality wines (<$15), let alone $20, though I suspect these wines are still ones Lynch loves to find; witness his own label Côtes du Rhône. I suspect one possible reason for the pivot to Italy over the last two decades had much to do with the potential to find more inexpensive quality wines there compared to France.
In the end, KLWM continues to provide a solid and consistent lineup of fine wines, if not as many affordable ones as in years past. That is the wine world we live in today. Kermit Lynch’s polestar guiding his selectivity is authenticity; the expression of place, the integrity of the producer, the ability to tell a true story about that producer which demonstrates their commitment to quality and personality. I hope Kermit himself and his wife, Gail Skoff, a fine photographer continue to enjoy their ‘retirement’ at their home in the south of France, the main reason I haven’t seen him in many years! But, as Kermit undoubtedly knows, you are never retired from the wine business. Salud!
A WORD ON THE NOTES BELOW
I didn’t include all of the wines tasted, leaving out some which were less excellent or whose price was simply too much in my opinion for the quality shown. There are some expensive wines included, for those of you aspiring wine drinkers who are willing to splurge and taste what I believe is a fine example; Spending this kind of $$ requires some guidance, I believe.
Wines are noted with one  to three \\\, though few wines truly reach Outstanding \\\.
Prices are approximate retail, based upon the wholesale prices offered by KLWM’s distributor here in Seattle. Grape names are often abbreviated as follows: PN= Pinot Noir; CH=Chardonnay; PM=Pinot Meunier; Gren=Grenache; Mour=Mourvedre; PG=Pinot Gris; PB= PInot Blanc; Syl=Sylvaner
FRANCE
Both of these small champagne houses produce excellent wines and very expressive of their respective base vineyard areas (e.g. Bouzy Grand Cru)
Champagne Paul Bara NV Brut Rose Grand Cru Bouzy, Champagne Grand Cru PN, CH Pale pink-salmon, Fresh berry nose & palate with lovely fruit, freshness and dry finish. Dis. 2/2025. Crisp mousse, lively and refreshing with excellent length and persistence. Now 2030 12.5% \\+ $88

Winter work on the slopes of Bouzy Grand Cru, 2014 (JBMW)
Champagne Nicolas Maillart NV Extra Brut Platine (Montagne de Reims), Champagne PN58, CH31, PM11 Premier Cru, 10 months aging in oak, Dis. 10/23 Dosage 2.5 gr/l Gold green. Delicate fine toast and appley red currant bouquet. Broader palate than above and richer texture. Fine mousse; creamier yet still dry finish with sappy, long finish. Now-2029 12.5% \\+
BURGUNDY
Burgundy is today where price and quality are both increasing IMO, but prices are increasing faster and higher to the point that us humble wine critics and normal people simply can no longer enjoy them. Still, there are wines which I strongly recommend, price excepted.
Henri Costal 2022 Chablis 1er Cru Vaillons, Chablis 1er Cru Chardonnay Fine stony-lees mineral rich bouquet with solid pear apple fruit. Refined, nutty finish and delicate oak shows class and depth. Medium body Great finish! Current market, this price is fair. Now-2034 12.5% \\(+) $59
Famille Savary 2023 Chablis Selection Vieilles Vignes, Chablis Chardonnay Less vanilla/lees toasty note and stonier than Costal above. Fine, mineral, flinty aromas lead into more of same on the palate, with a crystalline pure finish. Stylish and deep flavors. Almost good value in current market! Now-2030+. 12.5% \ $36
Domaine de Villaine 2023 Bouzeron Aligoté, Bouzeron Aligoté is the unsung, but increasingly praise-worthy white grape of Burgundy experiencing, at least in the village of Bouzeron, a return to favor. A grape that can age extremely well, too, if made with careful attention, as here. Rich, yellow fruit bouquet with some almond/filbert nutty notes. Moderate acidity, showing ripeness of the vintage and long finish. Classic and not simple. Too $$, but then again, it’s de Villaine! (one of the families that owns the famed Domaine de la Romanée-Conti) Now-2030. 13% \\- $54

De Villaine estate and garden with vineyards in Bouzeron on the hill, behind (JBMW, 2008)
Domaine de Villaine 2022 Rully 1er Cru Rabourcé, Rully 1er Cru Chardonnay Solid green yellow. Lovely mealy-toasty lees and oak-inflected bouquet with ripe pear/apple fruit. Long finish. Excellent focus and class, great fruit and refined richness. Probably quality equal to good Meursault 1er Cru, but too $$ for this AOP. Still, excellent/near outstanding. Now-2032. 14% \\(+) $120
Domaine de Villaine 2022 Bourgogne Rouge La Fortune Pinot Noir, earth-loam accents. Medium body. Rich chewy fruit; concentrated, pretty densely centeredr and firming tannins on finish. Potent yet fine, strong/savory finish. Needs time. Très cher for straight Bourgogne, but Serious Bourgogne! Now-2031+. 14% \ $60-78
Domaine Guillemot 2022 Savigny Les Beaune 1er Cru Les Serpentières Pinot Noir. 50% whole cluster fermented, planted 1946, aged in 20% new FO barrels. Medium ruby. Deeper, more focused bouquet to above; dark fruited, stony-licorice and black currant aromas, with loamy accents. Fine lengthy finish and refined tannins. Sappy, dense finish, evident savory-earthy accents, great fruit intensity and depth. Near outstanding SLB, if a bit pricy. Now-2034. 13.5% \\+ $80-90
René Bouvier 2022 Marsannay Longeroies Vieilles Vignes, Marsannay Pinot Noir. 70 year old vines, 50% whole cluster fermented and aged in 20% new French oak barrels Ruby. Substantial floral, black cherry aromas, gamy notes with less tea and stem. Full, rich, red fruit flavors revealing some savory-loamy notes and deep mid-palate fruit. Classy. Now-2032. 13.5% \ $66
Lucien Boillot 2022 Gevrey Chambertin Gevrey Chambertin Pinot Noir. 1957 planting. 30% whole cluster ferment, aged 30% new FO. Medium ruby. Strong raspberry, floral sour cherry bouquet with big fruitiness! Sappy and fresh, with fine elegant chewy finish and hint of ferrous-ness. Medium body Classy village wine with strong cassis mineral on finish adding definition. Expensive but excellent Village wine. Now-2032. 13.5% \\(+) $96-106

“Village” Vineyard in Gevrey Chambertin, with several important 1er Crus on the hillside behind town (JBMW 2008)
Lucien Boillot 2022 Gevrey Chambertin 1er Cru les Cherbaudes Gevrey Chambertin 1er Cru Pinot Noir. 1922 planting. As above production. Medium ruby. More complex, deeper, gamy -earth/loam bouquet with ripe black berry fruit aromas. Rich, yet subtle palate; denser texture, fine tannins very classy and more focused, layered finish. Clearly more depth as a 1er Cru, but Very $$- excellent for longer aging. Now-2035+. 13.5% \\+ $165-180
ALSACE
Domaine Kuentz-Bas NV Cremant d’Alsace Brut Pblanc 60%, Auxerrois 40% Good mousse, fresh lively fruit with light biscuity aromas and citruy flavors well balanced and long finish for style. GV. Now-2028. 12% \ $29
Domaine Meyer-Fonné 2024 Gentil d’Alsace, Alsace AOP PG, Aux, Syl, Ries. NO Gewürz! Fairly rich palate with subtle, smoky, goose fat (foie gras, anyone?) Auxerrois character evident. Good acid which refreshes the fullish palate. Finishes with a hint of pear. Well done blend. Now-2028. 12.5% \ $24
Domaine Ostertag 2022 Riesling Grand Cru Muenchberg, Alsace Grand Cru Gold green. Really granitic, minerally and firm finish, with notes of citrus oil and lemon peel. Good acidity. Dense not quite ferrous but quite tensile fresh flavors and solid length. Expensive. BUT excellent. Now-2035. 13.5% \\(+) $67-90
LOIRE VALLEY
Chateau d’Epire 2023 Savennières Chenin Blanc Strong, lanolin-quince & nutty bouquet at first. Broad, yet stony vibrant palate with stony finish. Young and fresh with length and potential, with quince and dried pear notes on finish. Now-2031. 12.5% \ $35
Domaine Roches Neuves (Thierry Germain) 2025 Saumur-Champigny AOP Cab Franc. Youthful ruby violet. Fresh & intense black berry, cedar-graphite and gamy bouquet with a light edge of pyrazines. Rich fruit, firm acidity and fine-grained tannins with moderate tannins and classy CF earthy-cedar ac
